rv.q: The play touches genre after genre, constantly twisting itself, always entertaining, and finally becoming its own weird and extraordinary thing: stunningly political and superbly theatrical.
A brilliantly bold and ferociously intelligent drama about our slippery times.
Lucy Prebble’s galvanising, messy, vital play is based on Luke Harding’s book about the killing of Alexander Litvinenko.
It’s an evening that instructs as it entertains and that leaves one appalled at Britain’s initial reluctance to do anything that might antagonise Moscow.
It is, however, as tender as it is clever, as incensed as it is inventive. It's a wonderful one-off.
It is a strange, funny and frequently exhilarating piece of theatre.
The problem is the play never hunts bigger game.
It's often funny or startling. But I didn't feel I learned much beyond the details reported from the public inquiry into this horrible murder.

As with that show, though, I find myself admiring the essential value of the piece – the necessity for it – more than the particulars of the theatrical approach; it once again feels as though a stark, horrifying story has been over-dressed.
Political, engaged theatre of such scope is rare; theatre that presents its case with such flair, power, humour and emotional punch is rarer still.
The evening is exhilarating not just for its intelligence but because of the risks it clearly takes, leaping from realism to surrealist cabaret, from gritty tragedy to slapstick.
Prebble has an amazing ability to translate true stories into compellingly alive theatrical experiences.
These details may sound chaotic and self-indulgent but the designs are high quality and the effects are always stimulating.
Smart as these devices are, “A Very Expensive Poison” is not nearly as wild a ride as it sounds — or, indeed, as it should be.

So there are kitschy song and dance routines and Spitting Image-style puppets of Stalin, Yeltsin and Gorbachev — while Reece Shearsmith’s Putin (above) pops up in the stalls to provide a sardonic running commentary. As well he might: the man got off scot-free.

cn.t: Prebble's inventive, shape-shifting play about Litvinenko's poisoning dazzles with theatrical flair and political urgency, though its meta approach and stylistic experimentation divide critics on whether the form enhances or overshadows the story.
